1.script: Everyone seemed to know the perfect way to use AI. Better prompts. Better tools. Better systems. The more confident the advice got, the less confident I felt.

2.script: Buy the course. Comment ‘AI agents.’ Get the perfect system. I was comparing myself to everybody else’s claims. So I changed the question: what actually works?

3.script: I’m Dave Sifry. I founded Technorati and co-founded Linuxcare. I got pissed with all those vibes. So I ran the tests. two thousand four hundred sixteen AI code reviews, across fifty pull requests and five mature open source codebases.

4.script: For the detailed comparison: I whittled it down to the six most knotty pull requests, Forty-two bugs humans had found. That gave me part of the answer. But humans are pretty bad at finding bugs!

5.script: After the audit: a hundred and five more verified defects. Each test failed before the fix and passed after. One hundred forty-seven bugs in the answer key.

6.script: A harness runs checks, assigns focused reviews in parallel, then combines findings. Same model, different jobs. I maintain metareview, one of the harnesses tested.

7.script: In matched comparisons, the harness found more verified bugs thirty-nine times out of forty-two. Same model. Same reasoning setting. The review process mattered.

8.script: Those extra passes used about ten times the tokens, at the median. More review has a price. Did that work also need an expensive model at high reasoning?

9.script: The reasoning dial is tempting. Turn it up, get a better review. But that’s an assumption. I tested low, medium and high to see what the extra thinking bought.

slideText: High vs. medium reasoning, original benchmark F1
10.script: Of twenty-two high-versus-medium comparisons, seventeen were inconclusive on the original benchmark score. Four favored high; one favored medium. Inconclusive doesn’t mean equal.

slideText: Verified bugs across the same six PRs, out of 147
11.script: One tested pair. Fable, high reasoning, one prompt: fifty-one bugs. Open-weight G L M Flash, low reasoning, a harness: seventy-one. Twenty more.

slideText: Mean API cost per review, at study list prices
12.script: About a dollar thirty versus two point four cents per review. API costs, at study prices. Checking the findings still takes your time.

13.script: Same pair: about two and a half minutes versus eighty seconds, on average. Less waiting. More bugs found. A combination worth testing in your development loop.

14.script: Even the highest-recall setup missed fifty-nine verified bugs. A clean review doesn’t prove the code is correct. Useful help. We still have to check.

15.script: Here’s one verified defect: re-importing a deleted post crashed. An isolated test reproduced it. Add the missing guard, and the test passes. Evidence you can check.

16.script: Run the review before you commit, while the changes are fresh. Put it in your normal development workflow. The goal: find defects before your users do.

17.script: Review the change. Reproduce the failure. Fix it. Run the test. Then review the fix, too. You’re responsible for checking the findings. The harness makes review repeatable.

18.script: Use a harness. Give the model focused review jobs and a repeatable process. In this study, that usually found more verified bugs than asking the same model once.

19.script: Start with low reasoning. Try open-weight models. Compare what they catch, what they miss, the cost and the wait. Then choose based on evidence from your code.

20.script: I started with doubt. Now I have evidence I can check. Demand that from AI advice, including mine. You don’t have to trust the vibes. Follow the evidence.
